title: The last line of defence against climate threats
full_text:
Global warming The public sector, regulators and policyholders themselves have a duty to manage the known unknowns, writes Alexandra Cain.
By 2050, more than 1.5 million Australians will live in areas that will experience serious sea-level rises and coastal flooding, according to the first National Climate Risk Assessment. This is on top of the thousands of businesses operating in these zones that could be wiped out.
Climate change's potential scale makes it tough for insurers to accurately price premiums, which have to accommodate still unknown risks. Nevertheless, regulators expect the insurance sector to be more upfront when the cost of policies rises steeply.
The unknown consequences of the potentially unstoppable collapse of the West Antarctic ice sheet show how difficult it is for communities, regulators and insurers to estimate environmental risks. Research shows even with little to no global warming, the West Antarctic ice sheet could contribute to a 4-metre rise in sea levels. While this could take centuries to play out, planning for a rise in sea levels must start now.
"I think we need to be really thoughtful about the way we go about this. There is a strong argument for industry alignment," IAG managing director and CEO Nick Hawkins told the Financial Review Insurance Summit in June.
Ugly concrete sea walls being built in places like Collaroy on the eastern seaboard, where homes teeter precariously on the oceanfront during big storms, serve as a warning.
"We do have a risk challenge in Australia, and it is a risk challenge that we are staring into now, but we should have stared into it well before now," says Lisa Harrison, chief executive of consumer insurance at Suncorp Group. "We are dealing with, unfortunately, homes built in the wrong places, homes not built to the right standards, and we have not invested enough in mitigation and resilience."
There needs to be more co-ordination between the public sector and regulators when planning new communities. The NSW state government is trying to bring different government departments and their policy instruments into one setting to make this happen. "It is also about the different layers of regulation, which often contradict each other or delay approval of development," says NSW Minister for Building Anoulack Chanthivong.
Looking ahead, the insurance sector is trying to find ways to calibrate policies so they reflect policyholders' real risks. For instance, there is a move to introduce a traffic-light system in policies so people and businesses are more aware of the environmental risks they face when they move or buy into a new neighbourhood.
"You can buy that first home, pay a big sum of money and not know that you are at high flood risk, bushfire risk or cyclone risk, and I do think that is a real problem," says Harrison.
Insurance is just one aspect of climate change risk mitigation and policyholders must take steps themselves to manage their premiums.
"The most effective way to manage insurance cost is to reduce the pricing of risk. This means policyholders controlling what they can via better resilience and presenting accurate underwriting data," says Marc Chiarella, CEO of risk advice firm Bellrock Advisory. "Insurance should really be the last line of defence, not the whole climate risk strategy."
Nevertheless, the insurance sector is working to make sure Australians, as well as businesses, can buy insurance they can afford, which responds after terrible storms, bushfires or other events. Much of this rests on helping people understand the protections their premium offers, which is something the insurance sector is working on. Regulators want to see a more consistent approach to explaining premium increases.
"If you look at what is driving consumer complaints to firms, based on the data that they report to ASIC, premiums are by far and away the biggest source of complaints and over two financial years, they more than tripled," says Alan Kirkland, commissioner at the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.
The Insurance Council of Australia is tackling this through changes to its code of conduct to bolster consumer protections as the sector grapples with climate change's unknowns.
"That the industry is moving towards a contractually enforceable code is going to be a significant step forward," says Daniel Mulino, Assistant Treasurer and federal Minister for Financial Services.AFR
